flawed_step: To prove it, you would need an exchange argument: any optimal solution can be changed step by step into the greedy one without losing value. That works for fractional knapsack, where you can take part of an item. It fails for 0/1 knapsack. An early high-ratio item can use capacity so that the leftover space is wasted, and you cannot take a fraction of a later item to fill it. So the step "the greedy choice is part of some optimal solution" cannot be justified.
counterexample: W = 10. Items: A (weight 6, value 7, ratio 7/6 ≈ 1.167), B (weight 5, value 5, ratio 1), C (weight 5, value 5, ratio 1). Greedy order is A, then B and C in either order (they tie). Greedy takes A (weight 6, 4 capacity left). B does not fit (5 > 4), and neither does C. Greedy total value = 7. The subset {B, C} has weight 10 <= 10 and value 10 > 7. So greedy is not optimal.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Greedy by value-to-weight ratio is optimal only for fractional knapsack, not 0/1 knapsack. The explicit instance above (W=10; items (6,7), (5,5), (5,5)) gives greedy value 7, but the best value is 10.
